docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.8+
  • pip

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Activate the virtual environment and install dependencies:

source venv/bin/activate
pip install mkdocs-material

docs.title: Local Development
docs.text:
Run the local dev server:

mkdocs serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser.

docs.title: Deploy to GitHub Pages
docs.text:
mkdocs gh-deploy

This builds the site and pushes it to the gh-pages branch automatically.

GitHub Pages Setup

Make sure GitHub Pages is configured to serve from the gh-pages branch in your repo settings under Settings → Pages.

docs.title: How kubeconfig Is Generated by Kubespray and k3d
docs.text: kubeconfig files tell kubectl (and other clients) how to reach a cluster and how to authenticate. By default, kubectl looks for a file named config in ~/.kube/, but tools like Kubespray and k3d generate and manage additional kubeconfigs for the clusters they create.[^1][^2][^3]

docs.title: Common kubeconfig concepts
docs.text:
A kubeconfig file is a YAML document containing:

  • clusters — API server endpoints and TLS settings.
  • users — credentials (client certificates, tokens, etc.).
  • contexts — a tuple of (cluster, user, namespace) to make a "profile".

kubectl chooses which cluster to talk to based on the current context. You can point it to a specific file by:

  • Setting KUBECONFIG=/path/to/kubeconfig, or
  • Using kubectl --kubeconfig=/path/to/kubeconfig ...[^4][^2][^5][^1]

docs.title: Kubespray: kubeconfig generation flow
docs.text: Kubespray is an Ansible playbook collection that installs a production-grade Kubernetes cluster on your own hosts. As part of the control-plane bootstrap, it generates kubeconfig files on the master/control-plane nodes and optionally on worker nodes.[^6][^7][^8]

docs.title: Where kubeconfig lives with Kubespray
docs.text:
On each control-plane node, Kubespray (via kubeadm) creates:

  • /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf — admin kubeconfig (cluster-admin privileges).
  • /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf — kubelet client config.
  • /etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf, scheduler.conf, etc.

Kubespray's docs note that kubeconfig files generally point to localhost on control-plane nodes, or to a local nginx proxy / external load balancer if configured.[^8][^6]

"The kubeconfig files generated will point to localhost (on kube_control_planes) and kube_node hosts will connect either to a localhost nginx proxy or to a loadbalancer if configured."[^6]

Practically:

  • Control-plane nodes talk to the API server via https://127.0.0.1:6443 (or a local proxy).
  • Worker nodes may point at a local nginx proxy or a dedicated external load balancer.[^8][^6]

docs.title: How Kubespray generates kubeconfig
docs.text:
1. kubeadm init on the first control-plane node

    kubeadm generates a CA and server/client certificates, then writes admin.conf and other component configs under /etc/kubernetes/.[^9][^8]

  2. Ansible templates and copies kubeconfig

    Kubespray's Ansible roles read admin.conf and adjust the server: field to point to either https://127.0.0.1:6443 or an HA load balancer.[^6][^8]

  3. Expose kubeconfig to the operator machine (manual step)

    Copy the file from the control-plane node to your workstation:

    scp ubuntu@cp-1:/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/kubeconfigs/admin.conf
export KUBECONFIG=~/kubeconfigs/admin.conf
kubectl get nodes

    Or merge it into ~/.kube/config using kubectl config commands.[^2][^4]

  4. Using kubeconfig on the control-plane node directly

    SSH to a control-plane node and run:

    export KUBECONFIG=/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
kubectl get nodes

    This talks to the API server bound to 127.0.0.1:6443 on that host.[^8][^6]

docs.title: Key characteristics of Kubespray kubeconfig
docs.text:
• Source of truth is admin.conf produced by kubeadm on the first control-plane node.[^9][^8]
  • Transport is https with client certs (cluster-admin credentials).
  • Endpoints are typically localhost or a configured load balancer.[^6][^8]
  • Distribution to operators is a manual step — Kubespray does not write kubeconfig on your laptop.

docs.title: k3d: kubeconfig generation flow
docs.text: k3d runs k3s (a lightweight Kubernetes distribution) inside Docker containers. Unlike Kubespray, it has direct control over both the control-plane and the CLI environment, so it can generate and update kubeconfigs on the fly.[^10][^11]

docs.title: Where kubeconfig lives with k3d
docs.text:
By default, k3d integrates with your existing kubeconfig:

  • It detects the "default" kubeconfig as the file pointed to by KUBECONFIG (if it references exactly one file), or ~/.kube/config if KUBECONFIG is unset.[^11][^10]

k3d can also:

  • Write a cluster-specific kubeconfig to ~/.k3d/kubeconfig-<cluster-name>.yaml.[^11]
  • Merge cluster details into your default kubeconfig and optionally switch context.

docs.title: How k3d generates kubeconfig during cluster creation
docs.text:
When you run k3d cluster create mycluster, the steps are:

  1. k3s server inside Docker creates its own kubeconfig

    k3s writes /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml inside the container, containing the API endpoint and certs.[^12]

  2. k3d reads and adapts that kubeconfig

    k3d inspects the container, reads the internal kubeconfig, and rewrites the server: URL to a host-accessible endpoint (e.g., https://0.0.0.0:<mapped-port>).[^11]

  3. k3d writes or merges kubeconfig on the host

    By default (k3d v5.x+), --kubeconfig-update-default is enabled:[^11]

    • Merges the new cluster into ~/.kube/config (or $KUBECONFIG).
    • Does not switch context unless you also pass --kubeconfig-switch-context.
    kubectl config get-contexts   # shows k3d-mycluster

docs.title: k3d kubeconfig commands
docs.text:
Write a standalone kubeconfig file:

k3d kubeconfig write mycluster
# creates ~/.k3d/kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml

Print to stdout and use directly:

k3d kubeconfig get mycluster > ./kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml
export KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml
kubectl get nodes

Merge into another file after creation:

k3d kubeconfig merge mycluster --output some/other/file.yaml
# or into default kubeconfig:
k3d kubeconfig merge mycluster --kubeconfig-merge-default

Add --kubeconfig-switch-context to make the new cluster the current context.[^10][^11]

docs.title: Example flows with k3d
docs.text:
Default behavior — merge into ~/.kube/config

k3d cluster create mycluster
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config use-context k3d-mycluster
kubectl get nodes

Standalone kubeconfig only

k3d cluster create mycluster --kubeconfig-update-default=false
k3d kubeconfig write mycluster
export KUBECONFIG=~/.k3d/kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml
kubectl get nodes

Useful for isolating cluster configs in scripts or demos.[^10][^11]

docs.title: Key characteristics of k3d kubeconfig
docs.text:
• Automatic — k3d always has a kubeconfig per cluster; merge or write standalone.[^11]
  • Context management — optionally switch context via --kubeconfig-switch-context.[^10][^11]
  • Host-visible endpoint — rewrites the server: URL from the k3s internal address to a host-reachable address/port.

docs.title: Summary: Kubespray vs k3d
docs.text:
Aspect Kubespray k3d Primary environment Bare-metal/VM hosts k3s inside Docker (local/dev) Where kubeconfig is created /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf via kubeadm Inside k3s container, exported to host Default endpoint https://127.0.0.1:6443 or nginx/LB Host-reachable mapped Docker port How operator gets kubeconfig Manual copy from node Auto-merged into default kubeconfig Integration with ~/.kube/config Not automatic Automatic (unless disabled) Context switching Manual via kubectl config use-context Optional via --kubeconfig-switch-context

Both tools produce standard kubeconfig files — the main differences are where they originate and how much automation they provide for placing and merging them.[^6][^11]
